segments.say: As the train gathers speed again, Oskar finds himself thinking about his sister, who showed him a scan picture of her baby a few months before it was born. A grey curve, a tiny hand, the outline of a face. What he didn't know then is that if the scan had run long enough, he might well have watched his nephew yawn.

Babies yawn before they're born. Doctors and researchers watching ultrasound images have noticed it for years: the jaw opens slowly, stays wide for a moment, and closes more quickly. It has the same lopsided shape as the yawn you did this evening. And this happens in someone who is surrounded by fluid and has never taken a single breath of air.

show.sub: Long before the first breath of air

segments.say: That last detail is worth pausing over. A baby in the womb receives oxygen through the placenta. Opening its mouth wide doesn't bring in any air at all. So whatever a fetal yawn is doing, it can't be fetching oxygen in the way the popular story describes. It's another quiet reason to doubt that fetching air is the whole point of the movement.

But how do you know a fetal yawn really is a yawn, and not just a mouth opening? In 2012, Nadja Reissland and her colleagues set out to separate the two. They used four-dimensional ultrasound, which is moving three-dimensional imaging, to watch fifteen healthy fetuses, eight girls and seven boys, at roughly twenty-four, twenty-eight, thirty-two and thirty-six weeks of pregnancy.

show.who: Nadja Reissland, Brian Francis and James Mason

segments.say: The key was timing. In a yawn, the opening phase takes noticeably longer than the closing phase. The researchers measured how long each mouth movement spent opening, holding and closing, and used that to sort true yawns from other openings. Across fifty-eight scans, they counted fifty-six yawns and twenty-seven mouth openings that didn't have the yawning shape. Almost all the yawns showed that slow rise clearly.

show.title: Telling a yawn from an open mouth
items: An ordinary mouth opening lacks that shape

segments.say: A folded knitted blanket and a pair of very small socks, laid out and waiting. There's something touching about the thought that one of the first things a person ever does with their face is also one of the things we'll do on the last tired evening of an ordinary week. The yawn is with us from the very beginning.

There was also a change over time. The average number of yawns observed fell from about two at twenty-four weeks to fewer at each later visit, and none were counted at the thirty-six week scans. The ordinary mouth openings declined with age too. Girls and boys didn't differ. The authors suggested this changing pattern might reflect how the brain is maturing.

show.title: Fetal yawns between 24 and 36 weeks
show.label: the average count fell steadily to none at the last scan

segments.say: Again, a note of caution. This was fifteen fetuses, watched for limited stretches of time. Not seeing a yawn during a scan doesn't mean a baby never yawns at that stage, and newborns certainly yawn. What the study offers is a careful way to identify fetal yawns and an early hint that their frequency changes during pregnancy. Larger studies would help to fill in the picture.

So why would anyone yawn in the womb? One idea is that the movement plays some part in development, perhaps in the growth of the jaw or in the maturing of the brain areas that control it. Many movements that will later be useful are rehearsed before birth. For yawning, these remain suggestions. The honest answer is that we don't yet know.

Once babies arrive, yawning is unmistakable. Anyone who has held a newborn has probably watched that tiny face open into an enormous, serious yawn, often followed by a little shudder and a return to sleep. They haven't copied it from anyone. They're too young for that, as we'll see later. This is the spontaneous yawn in its purest form, built in from the start.

Look at how wide the range is now. Before birth, in the first days of life, on waking, before sleep, during dull half hours, and perhaps before nerve-racking moments. Any explanation of spontaneous yawning needs to live comfortably with all of these. That's a demanding test, and it's one reason the question has stayed open for so long.

show.title: One behaviour, many moments
items: In the first days of life

segments.say: One family of explanations says yawning helps regulate arousal, meaning how alert and activated the brain is. The deep breath, the stretch of the jaw and the quickening heart might help nudge the system when it's sagging, or help it through a change of state. It fits the daily peaks, the dull viewing and the backstage nerves reasonably well.

The difficulty is showing that a yawn changes your alertness in a lasting way. The changes in heart rate and breathing that researchers record are brief, and some of them look like the ordinary effects of any very deep breath. If a yawn is a wake-up call, it seems to be a short one. Oskar can confirm that his last yawn didn't leave him feeling like a new man.

show.sub: Does it actually wake you up?

segments.say: Another family of ideas looks outward. A yawn is very visible and, often, audible. Perhaps in group-living animals it carries information: I'm winding down, I'm waking up, my state is changing. If others pick up that signal and shift along with it, a group might stay better in step. We'll return to this when we meet some lions, who have plenty to say on the subject.

It's worth remembering that these ideas aren't necessarily rivals. A behaviour that's very old can end up serving several purposes. It might help with a bodily adjustment in a single animal and also, in social species, work as a cue to others. Insisting on exactly one purpose may be asking nature to be tidier than it usually is.

show.text: An old movement may serve more than one purpose
show.by: A reasonable way to hold the question

segments.say: Oskar's phone buzzes. It's a short video from his sister: the baby, now four months old, yawning on a play mat, one fist waving. Oskar watches it, smiles, and feels the familiar stretch beginning. A baby too young to catch yawns has just handed one to his uncle through a telephone. The traffic, for now, only goes one way.

So far from the womb we've learned that fetuses yawn without any air to breathe, that a yawn can be told apart by its slow opening, and that in one small study the count fell as pregnancy went on. The purpose remains open. But there's one idea about purpose that has drawn a lot of attention, and it involves something unexpected.

show.title: Where we are
items: True yawns have a slow opening
Their number fell during pregnancy in one study

segments.say: The idea is that yawning helps to cool the brain. It sounds odd the first time you hear it. A yawn as a kind of ventilation, not for oxygen but for heat? Yet it leads to some testable predictions, and researchers have tried them out with warm packs, cold packs, careful breathing, and questions put to strangers on city streets.
